london_system.name: London System
london_system.summary: A solid, easy-to-learn opening. You play the same setup almost every game. Bishop out before e3 — that's the golden rule.
golden_rules: Bishop to f4 first, before e3. Always.
Don't trade your dark bishop unless you get something big.
Your dream setup: d4, e3, Bf4, Nf3, Bd3, O-O.
After setup is done, push for e4.

traps.name: Englund Gambit Trap
traps.description: They play 1...e5 trying to trick you. Take the pawn and win.
traps.trap_idea: They try to grab your b2 pawn with their queen. Let them — then trap the queen.
traps.how_to_avoid: Just play normal development. Their queen gets stuck.

traps.name: Bg4 Pin Trick
traps.description: They pin your knight spot with Bg4. You have a strong response.
traps.trap_idea: Push h3 then g4 to kick their bishop, then jump Ne5.
traps.how_to_avoid: Don't panic when they play Bg4. h3 then g4 is strong.

traps.name: Queen Trap after c5
traps.description: They take b2 with their queen. Nb5 and Rb1 traps it.
traps.trap_idea: Let them take b2. Their queen has no escape.
traps.how_to_avoid: Make sure you have Nb5 before allowing Qxb2.

d4.hint: What's the strongest first move to grab the center?
d4.right_feedback: Good — d4 grabs the center. Now think about your bishop.

d5.name: Main Line
d5.idea_opponent: They take their share of the center. Fair game.
d5.hint: Which piece should come out BEFORE you play e3?
d5.right_feedback: Exactly — Bf4 before e3. Golden rule of the London.
d5.wrong_feedback: In the London, the bishop MUST come to f4 before e3.

Nf6.name: Indian Setup
Nf6.hint: Same question as always — which piece first?
Nf6.right_feedback: Bf4 — doesn't matter what they play, bishop first.

c5.name: Early c5
c5.hint: They attacked your center. What's the calm response?
c5.right_feedback: e3 — stay calm. Your center holds.

Qb6.hint: Their queen eyes b2. How do you develop AND set a trap?
Qb6.right_feedback: Nc3 — if they take b2, Nb5+Rb1 traps their queen.

e5.name: Englund Gambit
e5.idea_opponent: A trick! They sacrifice a pawn hoping you blunder.
e5.hint: They offered a pawn. Should you take it?
e5.right_feedback: Take it. The Englund Gambit is bad for Black if you play correctly.
e5.wrong_feedback: Take the pawn! dxe5 is strong.

Bf5.name: Mirror London
Bf5.hint: They mirrored your London. Change your plan?
Bf5.right_feedback: e3 — stick to the plan. You have more space.

when_ahead.plan: Push e4 to open the center. Trade off defensive pieces.
ideas: Knight on e5 is a monster

when_equal.plan: Aim for e4. If blocked, play on the queenside with a4-a5.

when_behind.plan: Keep it closed. d4+e3 is hard to break. Wait for their mistake.

endgame_tips: d4+e3 structure is solid in endgames.
Activate your king early.
Push passed pawns.

italian_game.name: Italian Game
italian_game.summary: A classic opening. Develop quickly, point your bishop at f7, and attack the king. Simple and dangerous.
golden_rules: Bishop to c4 — aim at f7, the weakest square.
c3 prepares d4 — the ideal center.
Castle before attacking.
Don't grab pawns if it loses time.

traps.name: Fried Liver Attack
traps.description: Knight goes to g5 attacking f7. If they take, you sacrifice the knight for a devastating attack.
traps.trap_idea: After Nxf7, their king is dragged out. The attack is crushing.
traps.how_to_avoid: Black should play d5 instead of allowing Ng5.

traps.name: Legal's Mate
traps.description: Sacrifice the queen to deliver checkmate with minor pieces.
traps.trap_idea: If they take your queen with Bxd1, you play Bxf7+ Ke7 Nd5#. Checkmate!
traps.how_to_avoid: Don't take the queen if you see Bxf7+ coming.

traps.name: Blackburne Shilling Gambit
traps.description: Black plays Nd4 hoping you grab f7. Don't — just take the knight.
traps.trap_idea: Bxf7+ looks tempting but wastes your bishop. Nxd4 wins a piece.
traps.how_to_avoid: Don't be greedy. Nxd4 is simple and strong.

Nc6.name: Defending e5
Nc6.wrong_feedback: If you want the Italian Game, Bc4 is the move — aim at f7. Bb5 is the Ruy Lopez; d4 is the Scotch. Both fine, just different openings.

Bc5.name: Giuoco Piano
Bc5.hint: Prepare d4 with a pawn first.
Bc5.right_feedback: c3 — prepares d4. The big center is coming.
Bc5.wrong_feedback: In the Italian Game, the idea is: c3 prepares d4 — that's how you build the big center. Playing d4 immediately lets Black trade with exd4, hitting your knight and equalizing. d3 (the Giuoco Pianissimo / Italian Modern) is the quieter alternative — also OK if you prefer slow play, but c3 is the classical main line.

Nf6.name: Italian Main Line
Nf6.hint: Now you can play the central break.
Nf6.right_feedback: d4 — supported by c3. Now the big center is yours.
Nf6.wrong_feedback: In the Italian Game, d4 is the plan c3 was preparing. Anything else (b4 — Evans Gambit accepted is theoretically fine but a different opening; O-O — playable but lets Black play d6+ and consolidate) lets Black equalize.

exd4.name: Italian — d4 accepted
exd4.right_feedback: cxd4 — recapture with the c-pawn, building the big center.

Bb4+.name: Italian — Bb4+ check
Bb4+.idea_opponent: Black checks, hoping to disrupt your development.
Bb4+.right_feedback: Nc3 — block with the knight, accept the trade (or Bd2). Don't move the king.
Bb4+.wrong_feedback: In the Italian Game after cxd4 Bb4+, Nc3 is the natural block — develops a piece AND meets the check. Bd2 (Möller Attack variations) is also fine if you want sharper play. Don't play Kf1 (loses castling) or Kd2 (insane).

Nge7.name: Hungarian-like setup with Nge7
Nge7.idea_opponent: Unusual — knight to e7 instead of f6.
Nge7.wrong_feedback: Against Black's passive Nge7, d4 immediately is fine — Black can't easily challenge the center with the knight on e7 (blocks the e-pawn). Calm Italian setup play wins here.

Be7.name: Hungarian Defense
Be7.idea_opponent: Black plays the solid, passive Hungarian.
Be7.hint: Black's setup is too quiet — strike the center immediately.
Be7.right_feedback: d4 — open the center. The Hungarian doesn't fight for it; punish that.
Be7.wrong_feedback: Against the Hungarian Defense (...Be7), d4 immediately is the principled punishment — Black's quiet bishop on e7 lacks coordination with the rest of the army. d3 (slow Italian) is fine but lets Black equalize. d4 demands accuracy from Black.

Nf6.name: Two Knights Defense
Nf6.idea_opponent: Black plays more actively, eyes e4.
Nf6.right_feedback: Ng5 — attacks f7! Black must defend with d5 or face the Fried Liver.
Nf6.wrong_feedback: In the Two Knights Defense, Ng5 attacks f7 directly. d3 is the quiet Modern Italian (safer); d4 leads to the Max Lange or Scotch Gambit transpositions. Pick your style — but avoid Nc3 which lets Black equalize easily with d5.

d5.name: Two Knights — d5
d5.idea_opponent: Black blocks the diagonal, counter-attacks the bishop.

Nxd5.name: Fried Liver setup
Nxd5.idea_opponent: Black recaptures with the knight — walks into the Fried Liver.
Nxd5.right_feedback: Nxf7! — the Fried Liver Attack. Black's king is exposed.
Nxd5.wrong_feedback: After exd5 Nxd5, Nxf7 is THE move — the Fried Liver. Any other move lets Black escape. The point: Black's knight on d5 IS undefended; Nxf7 forces Kxf7 (the king can't run), then Qf3+ regains material and continues the attack.

Na5.name: Polerio Defense
Na5.idea_opponent: Black hits the bishop, sidestepping the Fried Liver.
Na5.right_feedback: Bb5+ — check, keeps the bishop active.
Na5.wrong_feedback: In the Polerio, Bb5+ is principled — give check first, develop with tempo. Retreating with Bb3 or Bf1 loses tempo. d3 (Bd3 next) is the quiet alternative — playable but less ambitious.

Nd4.name: Fritz Variation
Nd4.right_feedback: c3 — kick the knight, regain control of the center.
Nd4.wrong_feedback: In the Two Knights Fritz Variation, c3 kicks the d4 knight. Nxf7 here is INCORRECT (the knight on d4 isn't undefended like in the main line). c3 first, then the position becomes tactical.

when_ahead.plan: Open the center with d4. Attack the king.

when_equal.plan: Control d4 and d5. Keep bishops active.

when_behind.plan: Keep pieces active. Look for tactical tricks.
ideas: Don't trade into a bad endgame

endgame_tips: Bishop pair is strong in open endgames.
Central pawns are powerful.
Activate rooks on open files.

italian_game_black.name: Italian Game (Black side)
italian_game_black.summary: How to defend against the Italian Game (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4) as Black. Two main systems: Two Knights Defense (3...Nf6 — sharp, attacking the e-pawn back) or Giuoco Piano (3...Bc5 — mirror the bishop, classical). Both are sound; choice depends on whether you want sharp or quiet play.
golden_rules: Against 3.Bc4, Nf6 (Two Knights) is the sharpest reply — counter-attack the e-pawn.
Bc5 (Giuoco Piano) mirrors White's bishop — solid, equal-ish.
Watch for the Fried Liver — d5 to block White's Ng5 is critical.
Don't play Na5 to chase the bishop unless you know the Polerio theory cold.

Bc4.name: Italian Game
Bc4.idea_opponent: White aims the bishop at f7.
Bc4.hint: Two Knights (sharp) or Bc5 (classical)? Nf6 is the most ambitious.
Bc4.right_feedback: Nf6 — the Two Knights Defense. Counter-attack e4. Sharper play ahead.
Bc4.wrong_feedback: Against the Italian (3.Bc4), Nf6 is the Two Knights Defense — counter-attacks White's e-pawn, leads to sharp tactical play (including the Fried Liver if White goes for it). Bc5 is the Giuoco Piano — mirror White's bishop, classical/equal. Both sound; Nf6 if you want sharper games.

Ng5.name: Italian — Fried Liver Attack
Ng5.idea_opponent: White attacks f7 with the knight!
Ng5.hint: Block the diagonal AND attack White's bishop. One move that does both?
Ng5.right_feedback: d5 — defend f7 by blocking the diagonal, AND counter-attack the bishop. The critical defense.
Ng5.wrong_feedback: Against 4.Ng5 (Fried Liver Attack), d5 is THE critical defense — blocks Bc4's diagonal at f7 AND attacks the bishop. Without d5, White plays 5.Nxf7 and your king is gutted. Other moves (Bc5, Nxe4) lose to the Fried Liver. d5 is mandatory.

exd5.name: Two Knights — d5 accepted
exd5.hint: DON'T recapture with the knight — that's the Fried Liver trap. Hit the bishop instead.
exd5.right_feedback: Na5 — the Polerio Defense. Attacks the bishop, sidesteps the Fried Liver.
exd5.wrong_feedback: After 5.exd5, Na5 (Polerio Defense) is the principled move — hits Bc4 with tempo, avoids the Fried Liver entirely. Nxd5 here is the Fried Liver trap — White plays Nxf7! winning material. Na5 is sound; Nxd5 is unsound unless you've memorized the Lolli/Traxler refutation lines.

d3.name: Italian — Modern (d3) / Giuoco Pianissimo
d3.idea_opponent: White plays the quiet Modern Italian — slow, positional.
d3.right_feedback: Bc5 — mirror White's bishop, classical setup. Equal positional game ahead.
d3.wrong_feedback: Against the Modern Italian (d3), Bc5 is the classical reply — mirror the bishop. d6 is also fine (Pirc-like). The Modern Italian is quiet; both sides have similar plans and the game is decided in the middlegame.

when_equal.plan: In the Italian as Black, the typical middlegame plan is queenside expansion (a6 + b5 + Bb7) while White attacks on the kingside. Trade pieces if needed.
ideas: Develop pieces actively, especially the c8 bishop via b7 or g4.
Castle kingside, then expand on the queenside with a6 + b5.
Watch for White's d4 break — meet it with exd4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 cxd4 etc.

when_ahead.plan: Trade down. The Italian as Black usually reaches equal or slightly worse positions; if you're ahead, trade pieces and aim for the endgame.

when_behind.plan: Defend solidly — the Italian rarely produces forced losing lines from Black's side. Keep the position closed.

endgame_tips: Bishop endgames where you have the bishop pair are technically winning if you have any advantage.
Rook endgames after the Italian are often dry — know your Lucena and Philidor positions.

sicilian_defense.name: Sicilian Defense
sicilian_defense.summary: The sharpest response to e4. You fight for the center with c5 instead of e5. Leads to rich, complex positions.
golden_rules: c5 fights for d4 without committing your e-pawn.
You're playing for a queenside counter-attack.
Don't be scared of White's kingside attack — you attack queenside.
d6 + Nf6 is the solid setup.

traps.name: Siberian Trap
traps.description: Black plays Qa5 pinning the knight and threatening Bxc3+.
traps.trap_idea: White's knight on c3 is pinned. If they don't see it, you win material.
traps.how_to_avoid: White should play Bd2 or Nb3 to break the pin.

traps.name: Magnus Smith Trap
traps.description: White plays Bc4 and after Bg7, Nd5! forks everything.
traps.trap_idea: The knight on d5 attacks multiple pieces. Black's in trouble.
traps.how_to_avoid: Black should delay Bg7 and play a6 or e6 first.

e4.hint: What move fights for d4 from the flank, avoiding symmetry?
e4.right_feedback: c5 — the Sicilian. Most ambitious response to e4.
e4.wrong_feedback: In response to 1.e4, c5 is the Sicilian — most ambitious for Black, sets up unbalanced play. e5 invites the Open Game (Italian / Ruy Lopez / Scotch), e6 the French, c6 the Caro-Kann, d6 Pirc/Modern. All sound; c5 is the most fighting.

Nf3.name: Sicilian — Open setup begins
Nf3.idea_opponent: White's most popular move, preparing d4.
Nf3.hint: Flexible Najdorf-style setup — prepare Nf6 and later a6.
Nf3.right_feedback: d6 — supports e5 push, prepares Nf6.
Nf3.wrong_feedback: Against 2.Nf3, d6 is the most flexible — leads to Najdorf / Classical / Dragon depending on Black's later choices. Nc6 commits to the Classical / Sveshnikov lines. e6 leads to Taimanov / Kan / Paulsen. All sound; d6 is the most-played at top level.

d4.name: Open Sicilian
d4.right_feedback: cxd4 — trade pawns, open the c-file for queenside play.

Nc3.name: Open Sicilian — Nc3
Nc3.hint: Najdorf or Classical? a6 commits you to one of the most-studied openings in chess.
Nc3.right_feedback: a6 — the Najdorf. Prepare b5 + Bb7, fight on the queenside.
Nc3.wrong_feedback: In the Najdorf Sicilian, a6 prepares b5 + Bb7 — fighting on the queenside. Nc6 here would be the Classical Sicilian (different plan: knight to c6, dark-square strategy). g6 leads to the Dragon (sharp, double-edged). All sound; if you want the Najdorf, a6 is the move.

Be3.name: Najdorf — English Attack
Be3.idea_opponent: White plays the sharp English Attack — Be3, f3, g4, h4, attacking the kingside.
Be3.hint: Strike back in the center before White's pawn storm arrives.
Be3.right_feedback: e5 — closes the center, kicks the d4 knight, fights for d5 outpost.
Be3.wrong_feedback: In the Najdorf English Attack, e5 is the principled central break — closes the center BEFORE White's kingside storm gets going. Nf6 already played; e6 (Scheveningen-style) is playable but invites a faster White attack. e5 is sharp but theoretically sound.

Bg5.name: Najdorf — Bg5
Bg5.idea_opponent: White plays the aggressive Bg5 main line.
Bg5.right_feedback: e6 — solidify the kingside, prepare Be7.
Bg5.wrong_feedback: Against the Bg5 Najdorf, e6 is the most-played response — solid, prepares ...Be7. ...Nbd7 is also OK but less precise. e5 (which works against English Attack) is INFERIOR here because Bg5 pins the f6 knight and the e5 push isn't easily prepared.

when_ahead.plan: Push on the queenside with a5-a4, b5-b4. Open the a and b files.
ideas: Your bishops are strong on long diagonals

when_equal.plan: Control d5 and fight for the center.
ideas: Knights on c6 and d4 are strong

when_behind.plan: Complicate. The Sicilian is a fighting opening.

endgame_tips: Your queenside pawns can be dangerous.
The Sicilian often leads to opposite-side attacks.
King activity is key.

caro_kann.name: Caro-Kann Defense
caro_kann.summary: A solid, reliable response to e4. You play c6 then d5, challenging the center while keeping a solid pawn structure.
golden_rules: c6 then d5 — challenge the center solidly.
Get your bishop OUT before playing e6 (same idea as London!).
Your pawn structure is your strength.
Don't rush — the Caro-Kann is about patience.

traps.name: Caro-Kann Smothered Mate
traps.description: White plays Nd6# — smothered mate! Black's pieces block all escape squares.
traps.trap_idea: The knight on d6 delivers checkmate because Black's own pieces block the king.
traps.how_to_avoid: Black should not play Nd7 and Ngf6 without checking for Nd6.

e4.hint: What move builds a wall and prepares d5 with pawn support?
e4.right_feedback: c6 — the Caro-Kann. You'll play d5 with the c-pawn backing it up.

d4.name: Caro-Kann main
d4.right_feedback: d5 — challenge the center with pawn support from c6.

Nc3.name: Caro-Kann — Classical setup
Nc3.right_feedback: dxe4 — take the e-pawn, open lines for your light-square bishop.

Nxe4.name: Caro-Kann — Classical Main Line
Nxe4.hint: Now develop the light-square bishop — but where, before you lock in e6?
Nxe4.right_feedback: Bf5 — your bishop goes OUTSIDE the pawn chain, the defining Caro-Kann idea.
Nxe4.wrong_feedback: In the Caro-Kann Classical, Bf5 is the defining move — get your light-square bishop OUTSIDE the c6-d5-e6 pawn chain BEFORE you lock it in with e6. Playing Nd7 or Nf6 first traps the bishop inside the chain — the classic Caro-Kann mistake.

Ng3.name: Classical — Ng3 chasing the bishop
Ng3.right_feedback: Bg6 — keep the bishop's diagonal alive. Don't retreat further.
Ng3.wrong_feedback: In the Caro-Kann Classical after Ng3, Bg6 is correct — keeps the bishop active on the b1-h7 diagonal. Bd7 retreats too far (passive); Bh5? loses the bishop after h4-h5.

e5.name: Caro-Kann — Advance Variation
e5.idea_opponent: White locks the center, gains space, prepares kingside attack.
e5.hint: Get the light-square bishop OUT before you play e6.
e5.right_feedback: Bf5 — same defining idea as the Classical: bishop outside the chain before e6 locks it in.
e5.wrong_feedback: In the Caro-Kann Advance, Bf5 is the move — your light-square bishop MUST get out before e6 traps it. The Caro-Kann's main complaint about the French is the bishop-on-c8 problem; don't recreate it here. c5 (challenging the chain) is also fine but Bf5 first is more accurate.

exd5.name: Caro-Kann — Exchange Variation
exd5.idea_opponent: White trades and aims for a quiet game.
exd5.right_feedback: cxd5 — recapture with the c-pawn, leaving a symmetric structure.
exd5.wrong_feedback: In the Caro-Kann Exchange, cxd5 is correct — recapture with the pawn that has the better square afterward. Don't take with the queen (Qxd5 loses tempo to Nc3).

when_ahead.plan: Use your solid structure. Push pawns on the queenside.
ideas: Rooks on c and d files

when_equal.plan: Stay solid. The Caro-Kann is a fortress.
ideas: Knights on d5 or e4 outposts

when_behind.plan: Keep the position closed. Your structure is hard to break.

endgame_tips: Your pawn structure shines in endgames.
Bishop + pawns endgames favor you.
Passed c-pawn can be a winner.

french_defense.name: French Defense
french_defense.summary: Play e6 then d5. You let White take space but build a solid wall and counter-attack later.
golden_rules: e6 first, then d5 — challenge the center.
Your light bishop gets locked in. Find a way to activate it.
c5 is your key counter-strike against d4.
Be patient — the French is a slow burn.

traps.name: French Winawer Poisoned Pawn
traps.description: Black grabs the g2 pawn with Qg4. Risky but powerful if White doesn't know the theory.
traps.trap_idea: The g2 pawn is free and White's kingside is weak.
traps.how_to_avoid: White should protect g2 or play Qg4 prevention lines.

e4.hint: What move builds a solid wall, preparing d5?
e4.right_feedback: e6 — the French Defense. You'll strike with d5 next.

d4.name: French — Main
d4.right_feedback: d5 — challenge the e-pawn. White must commit to a setup.

Nc3.name: French — Classical / Winawer Setup
Nc3.idea_opponent: White defends e4 with a developing move.
Nc3.right_feedback: Nf6 — Classical French. Pressures e4, develops naturally.
Nc3.wrong_feedback: After 3.Nc3, Nf6 is the Classical French (most-played, solid). Bb4 is the sharp Winawer (gives up bishop pair for activity and pawn structure damage). dxe4 is the Rubinstein (passive but sound). All defensible; Nf6 is the main line.

e5.name: French — Steinitz Variation
e5.right_feedback: Nfd7 — knight retreats but keeps c5 break available.
e5.wrong_feedback: In the French Steinitz, Nfd7 is correct — preserves c5 break. Ng8 wastes development; Nh5? loses to g4 trapping the knight.

Bg5.name: French — McCutcheon / Classical Bg5
Bg5.right_feedback: Bb4 — counter-pin, the McCutcheon Variation. Sharp but theoretically sound.
Bg5.wrong_feedback: Against 4.Bg5 in the Classical French, Bb4 is the modern main line (the McCutcheon). Pins the c3 knight. Be7 is the older, quieter Classical Main Line — also playable but less ambitious. Don't break the pin with h6 (it just helps White: 5.Bxf6 trades pieces).

Nd2.name: French — Tarrasch Variation
Nd2.idea_opponent: White avoids the pin, plays Nd2 instead.
Nd2.right_feedback: Nf6 — same development as Classical, but White's structure is different.
Nd2.wrong_feedback: Against 3.Nd2 (Tarrasch), Nf6 is the modern main line. c5 (challenging the center immediately) is also popular and sharp. Both are sound; Nf6 keeps options open.

e5.name: French — Advance Variation
e5.idea_opponent: White locks the center, plans kingside attack.
e5.hint: Challenge the pawn chain at its base.
e5.right_feedback: c5 — the standard French break, hits the base of White's pawn chain.
e5.wrong_feedback: In the French Advance, c5 is THE move — challenge White's pawn chain at its base (d4). Without c5 you're left passive with no counterplay. f6 is the alternative break (Milner-Barry-Gambit territory if White accepts), sharp and theoretically OK but less common.

exd5.name: French — Exchange Variation
exd5.idea_opponent: White trades and aims for a quiet game.
exd5.right_feedback: exd5 — symmetric structure. The Exchange is dry but not equal.

when_ahead.plan: Break with c5 and open the position for your pieces.

when_equal.plan: Play c5 and look to free your light bishop.

when_behind.plan: Keep it closed. Your pawn chain is hard to break.

endgame_tips: Your pawn structure is solid.
The bad bishop problem disappears in endgames with trades.
King activity matters.

queens_gambit.name: Queen's Gambit
queens_gambit.summary: Offer a pawn with c4 to control the center. If they take, you get it back easily. Classic, strong, reliable.
golden_rules: c4 fights for d5 control.
If they take c4, don't panic — you get it back.
Bg5 pins the knight — classic pressure.
Control d5, then attack.

traps.name: Elephant Trap
traps.description: White takes d5 thinking it wins a pawn. But Nxe4! wins the bishop because of the pin.
traps.trap_idea: After Nxe4, White's bishop on g5 is attacked by the queen, and the knight on e4 forks.
traps.how_to_avoid: White should NOT play Nxd5 in this position.

d5.name: Closed Game
d5.hint: What's the gambit move that offers a pawn for development?
d5.right_feedback: c4 — the Queen's Gambit. Offers the c-pawn to break Black's pawn on d5.
d5.wrong_feedback: In the Queen's Gambit, c4 is the defining move — offer the c-pawn to break Black's pawn on d5. Without c4 you're playing a quiet Queen's Pawn Game (London / Colle / Torre), not the Queen's Gambit. Both fine, just different openings.

e6.name: Queen's Gambit Declined (QGD)
e6.idea_opponent: Black declines, builds a solid wall.

Nf6.name: QGD — Main Line
Nf6.hint: Develop the bishop actively, pin the f6 knight.
Nf6.right_feedback: Bg5 — pins the knight, pressures Black's center.
Nf6.wrong_feedback: In the QGD, Bg5 is the main attacking move — pins the f6 knight, indirectly pressuring d5. cxd5 (Exchange QGD) trades immediately — playable, leads to a clear positional game. Bf4 is the London-style setup. For classical QGD, Bg5 is canonical.

Be7.name: QGD — Classical Main
Be7.idea_opponent: Black breaks the pin with the bishop.
Be7.right_feedback: e3 — develop calmly, prepare Bd3 + Nf3 + O-O.

h6.name: QGD — Tartakower / Lasker prep
h6.idea_opponent: Black asks the bishop a question.
h6.right_feedback: Bxf6 — trade the bishop, give Black doubled pawns or compromise structure.
h6.wrong_feedback: After Black's ...h6 in the QGD, Bxf6 is the main move — Black recaptures with the queen (Qxf6) or gives up the bishop pair entirely. Bh4 (keeping the pin) is also fine but committed.

dxc4.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted (QGA)
dxc4.hint: Develop first, regain the pawn later.
dxc4.right_feedback: Nf3 — develop. The c4 pawn isn't going anywhere safely.
dxc4.wrong_feedback: In the QGA, Nf3 first is the modern way — develop before grabbing the pawn. Trying to win c4 immediately with Qa4+ is theoretically OK but creates an exposed queen. e3 (preparing Bxc4 next) is also fine. Develop, castle, THEN reclaim c4.

Nf6.name: QGA — Main
Nf6.right_feedback: e3 — prepare Bxc4 to regain the pawn.

c6.name: Slav Defense (transposition)
c6.right_feedback: Nf3 — develop, prepare to handle the Slav.

e5.name: Albin Counter-Gambit
e5.idea_opponent: Black sacrifices the pawn for sharp play — the Albin.
e5.right_feedback: dxe5 — accept the pawn. Now don't grab d5 with the bishop too greedily.
e5.wrong_feedback: Against the Albin Counter-Gambit, dxe5 is correct — take the pawn. The trap: don't play 4.e3 (allows Bb4+ + d3! and Black wins material). After dxe5, Black plays d4 and you continue with Nf3 to attack d4.

when_ahead.plan: Push e4 and open the center. Your pieces are better.
ideas: Push b4-b5 on the queenside to crack their pawns
Rooks on c and d files

when_equal.plan: Hold d5. Push b4-b5 to break their queenside pawn structure.

when_behind.plan: Simplify. Your pawn structure is usually good.
ideas: Don't let them attack your king

endgame_tips: Central pawns are strong.
Pushing b4-b5 on the queenside cracks their pawn structure and creates weak squares to land pieces on.
Rook endgames favor better structure.

scandinavian_defense.name: Scandinavian Defense
scandinavian_defense.summary: Immediately challenge e4 with d5. Simple, direct, and gets your queen active early.
golden_rules: Take the pawn back with your queen — Qd5 or Qd6.
Get your bishop out before e6 — same as London.
Qa5 is the safest queen square.
Develop quickly — your queen is already out.

traps.name: Portuguese Gambit Trap
traps.description: Instead of taking back the pawn, play Nf6 then Bg4, creating tactical pressure.
traps.trap_idea: Bg4 pins the queen to the king. If White plays Be2, Nxd5 wins the pawn back with activity.
traps.how_to_avoid: White should be careful about the pin and not play passively.

e4.hint: What move challenges the e-pawn immediately?
e4.right_feedback: d5 — the Scandinavian. Accept a tempo loss to rid the board of White's e-pawn.

exd5.name: Scandinavian — Main
exd5.hint: Recapture immediately with the queen (main line).
exd5.right_feedback: Qxd5 — accept the tempo loss for clear development.

Nc3.name: Scandinavian — Nc3 attacking the queen
Nc3.idea_opponent: White develops with tempo, attacking your queen.
Nc3.hint: Where does the queen go — safely active, not blocking your own pieces?
Nc3.right_feedback: Qa5 — keeps the queen active, doesn't block the d-file for your rook.
Nc3.wrong_feedback: In the Scandinavian, after 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3, Qa5 is the main retreat — keeps the queen active and out of trouble. Qd8 wastes the whole opening (gives back the tempo you bought with the queen excursion); Qd6 is playable but blocks the d-file for your rook.

when_ahead.plan: Your development lead matters. Open lines.

when_equal.plan: Solid development. Bf5, e6, c6 fortress.

when_behind.plan: Keep it solid. Your pawn structure is reliable.

endgame_tips: Your structure is solid.
Active queen gives endgame chances.
Don't let them control the d-file.

ruy_lopez.name: Ruy Lopez
ruy_lopez.summary: The king of openings. Bb5 puts pressure on Black's defense of e5. Deep, strategic, tested for centuries.
golden_rules: Bb5 doesn't try to WIN the e5 pawn — it puts long-term pressure.
Castle early, then build with c3+d4.
Re1 supports e4 and puts pressure on the e-file.
Be patient — the Ruy Lopez is a marathon, not a sprint.

traps.name: Noah's Ark Trap
traps.description: Black traps White's bishop on b3 with a5-a4. The bishop has nowhere to go.
traps.trap_idea: After a5, a4, the bishop is trapped by its own pawns.
traps.how_to_avoid: White should retreat the bishop to d5 or c2 early.

Nc6.right_feedback: Bb5 — the Spanish Bishop. Pressures the knight that defends e5.
Nc6.wrong_feedback: In the Ruy Lopez, Bb5 is the defining move — attack the defender of e5 directly. Bc4 leads to the Italian; here the idea is to pressure the knight that holds Black's center together.

a6.name: Morphy Defense
a6.idea_opponent: Black asks the bishop a question.
a6.right_feedback: Ba4 — keeps the pin. Black plays Nf6, you castle.
a6.wrong_feedback: In the Ruy Lopez, Ba4 keeps your pin on the c6-knight. Bxc6 is the Exchange Variation — playable but trades your bishop pair away. Ba4 is the main line at every level.

Nf6.name: Closed Ruy Lopez
Nf6.right_feedback: O-O — castle. The pin defends e4 indirectly (if Nxe4 then Re1 wins the knight back).
Nf6.wrong_feedback: In the Ruy Lopez Closed, O-O is correct — the pin on c6 means Nxe4 is unsafe for Black (Re1 pins). Don't waste time defending e4 with d3; castle first.

Be7.name: Closed Ruy — Main
Be7.idea_opponent: Black develops the bishop, prepares to castle.
Be7.hint: Defend e4 — the pin gets less reliable now that Black has developed.
Be7.right_feedback: Re1 — supports e4, prepares c3 + d4 expansion.
Be7.wrong_feedback: In the Ruy Lopez Closed Main, Re1 is the canonical move — supports e4 explicitly (the pin alone no longer suffices once Black develops). Then plan c3 + d4 to claim space. Bxc6 dxc6 here trades the bishop pair early — playable (Exchange Spanish lines) but less ambitious.

b5.name: Closed Ruy — b5 hitting the bishop
b5.idea_opponent: Black gains queenside space, kicks the bishop.
b5.right_feedback: Bb3 — bishop on its strongest diagonal, eyes f7.
b5.wrong_feedback: After Black's b5, Bb3 is correct — the bishop on b3 eyes f7 and stays useful. Ba4 is also OK but b5 already restricts it. Bxc6 would be premature here — wait for Black to commit further.

Nf6.name: Berlin Defense
Nf6.idea_opponent: Black attacks e4 immediately — the Berlin Wall.
Nf6.right_feedback: O-O — same idea. The pin defends e4.
Nf6.wrong_feedback: In the Ruy Lopez Berlin, O-O is correct — castles, lets Black take e4 if they want (Nxe4 d4 — White gets a strong center). d3 is the modern Anti-Berlin (safer but less ambitious).

Nxe4.name: Open Berlin
Nxe4.idea_opponent: Black grabs the pawn — the famous Berlin endgame setup.
Nxe4.right_feedback: d4 — open the position. The Berlin endgame is balanced but White has dynamic chances.
Nxe4.wrong_feedback: In the Open Berlin, d4 is the principled response — open the center to exploit the knight excursion. Re1 is also fine; both lead to the Berlin endgame after the queen trade. Anything passive lets Black consolidate the extra pawn.

when_ahead.plan: Push d4 and open the center.

when_equal.plan: Build slowly with c3, d4, Nbd2-f1-g3.
ideas: Maneuver knight to g3 or f5

when_behind.plan: Keep pieces active. The Ruy Lopez structure is resilient.

endgame_tips: The Ruy Lopez often leads to complex endgames.
Bishop pair is an advantage.
Central control wins endgames.

scotch_game.name: Scotch Game
scotch_game.summary: Open the center on move three. Sharper than the Italian. Trade in the middle and push the d-pawn.
golden_rules: d4 on move three — fight for the center immediately.
Trade in the centre, develop, then push.
Don't fear early queen trades — your pieces are more active.
Watch for c-file pressure and the Nf5 jump.

Nc6.hint: Open the center with a pawn break.
Nc6.right_feedback: d4 — the Scotch Game. Strikes the center immediately.
Nc6.wrong_feedback: In the Scotch Game, d4 is the defining move — open the center before Black gets organized. Bc4 leads to the Italian, Bb5 to the Ruy Lopez. Choose d4 for the Scotch.

exd4.name: Scotch — Main Line
exd4.wrong_feedback: In the Scotch, Nxd4 is the right recapture — the knight on d4 is excellent. Don't take with the queen (Qxd4) which lets Black gain tempo with Nc6 hitting your queen.

Bc5.name: Scotch Classical
Bc5.idea_opponent: Black eyes the knight and f2.
Bc5.right_feedback: Be3 — defends the knight, blocks Black's bishop.
Bc5.wrong_feedback: In the Scotch Classical, Be3 is the right defensive idea — supports d4 and blocks Black's bishop diagonal. Nxc6 just damages your own structure unnecessarily.

when_ahead.plan: Trade pieces. The d-pawn becomes a monster.

when_equal.plan: Keep pieces active. Look for c-file or e-file pressure.

when_behind.plan: Stay sharp. Avoid trades into a worse endgame.

endgame_tips: An advanced d-pawn is a winning weapon.
Bishop pair is strong with open files.
Centralise rooks before pushing.

petrov_defense.name: Petrov Defense
petrov_defense.summary: Black's most solid response to 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 — immediately counterattacks White's e-pawn instead of defending e5. Reputation: drawish but theoretically resilient. Used by GMs at the highest level to neutralize 1.e4 with minimal risk.
golden_rules: Counter-attack with Nf6 INSTEAD of defending e5 with Nc6.
After 3.Nxe5, retreat to d6 first — never play 3...Nxe4 without preparation.
The Petrov fights for symmetric structure; play accurately, don't try to win the opening.
Black's bishop pair is often the long-term asset — don't trade them away.

Nf3.hint: What if instead of defending e5, you ATTACK White's e-pawn?
Nf3.right_feedback: Nf6 — the Petrov Defense. Counter-attack instead of defending.
Nf3.wrong_feedback: After 2.Nf3, Nc6 is the classical defense (Italian / Ruy Lopez territory). Nf6 is the Petrov — counter-attacks e4 immediately. Both are sound; Petrov is the solid choice for players who want minimal opening risk.

Nxe5.name: Petrov Main Line
Nxe5.hint: DON'T play Nxe4 yet — White has Qe2 winning. Push the knight back first.
Nxe5.right_feedback: d6 — kicks the knight, prepares Nxe4 SAFELY next.
Nxe5.wrong_feedback: In the Petrov Main Line, d6 FIRST is critical — playing Nxe4 immediately loses to 4.Qe2! Nf6 5.Nc6+ winning the queen. Always push the knight away with d6 before recapturing e4. This is the famous Petrov trap.

Nf3.name: Petrov — Classical retreat
Nf3.right_feedback: Nxe4 — NOW you can safely take. The knight is no longer next to your queen.
Nf3.wrong_feedback: Now that the white knight has retreated to f3 (not threatening your queen via Nc6+), Nxe4 is safe and main line. You regain the pawn. Don't get fancy with anything else here.

when_equal.plan: Trade pieces for a symmetric endgame — your structure is sound. Aim for the bishop pair if possible. The Petrov plays for technique, not attack.
ideas: Trade queens when offered — the Petrov rewards technique.
Keep the bishop pair if you can; trade your worst minor for White's best.
If the position simplifies and you're not worse, you're doing well.

when_ahead.plan: Simplify decisively. The Petrov's solidity means White rarely creates winning chances — convert positional edges patiently.
ideas: Activate the rooks on open files.
Push the pawn majority in the endgame.

when_behind.plan: Play for the symmetric structure to dry the position out. The Petrov is famously hard to lose from equal positions.

endgame_tips: Symmetric pawn structures favor the side with the better minor pieces — keep your bishop pair active.
The Petrov often reaches rook endgames; learn the basic Lucena and Philidor positions.

kings_indian_defense.name: King's Indian Defense
kings_indian_defense.summary: Let White build a big centre, then smash it. Fianchetto, castle, push f5 and attack.
golden_rules: Fianchetto the bishop to g7 — long diagonal at the queenside.
Castle early, attack later. Safety first.
Push e5 (or c5) to challenge the centre.
When White locks the centre, your f5 break is the main plan.

d4.hint: What's the universal knight move against d4?
d4.right_feedback: Nf6 — flexible. Develops, attacks the e4 square.

c4.name: KID setup begins
c4.hint: Prepare the fianchetto — King's Indian Defense.
c4.right_feedback: g6 — the King's Indian Defense. Fianchetto coming.
c4.wrong_feedback: In the King's Indian Defense, g6 is the defining move — preparing the fianchetto bishop on g7. e6 here leads to the Nimzo-Indian or QGD (different opening, different plans). For the KID, g6 commits you to the hypermodern setup.

Nc3.name: KID — Main Line
Nc3.right_feedback: Bg7 — completes the fianchetto, eyes the long diagonal.

e4.name: KID — Classical Main (vs e4 setup)
e4.hint: Prepare the central counter-strike with e5 later.
e4.right_feedback: d6 — supports e5 break, the soul of the KID.
e4.wrong_feedback: In the King's Indian Defense, d6 is the principled preparation for the e5 break — the entire KID plan revolves around striking e5 against White's center. d5 here closes the center prematurely (you'd be playing a worse Grünfeld).

Nf3.name: KID — Classical Mainline
Nf3.right_feedback: O-O — get the king safe before launching the kingside attack.

Be2.name: KID — Classical Setup
Be2.idea_opponent: White's bishop goes to a quiet square; main line ahead.
Be2.right_feedback: e5 — the KID break. White must decide: close with d5 (main) or trade.
Be2.wrong_feedback: In the KID Classical, e5 is the standard central strike — fights for d4, opens lines for the dark-square bishop on g7. Without e5, the KID is just a passive setup. After e5, plan Nbd7 + a5 + Nh5 — the kingside attack.

f3.name: KID — Sämisch Variation
f3.idea_opponent: White plays the Sämisch — solid pawn shield for the king, plans kingside castle and attack.
f3.right_feedback: O-O — castle into safety; the Sämisch is slow, you have time.
f3.wrong_feedback: Against the Sämisch (f3), O-O first is the modern main line — get safe, then play c5 or e5 break depending on White's setup. Nc6 too early can be met with d5; e5 is also OK and immediate. O-O keeps maximum flexibility.

g3.name: KID — Fianchetto Variation
g3.idea_opponent: White mirrors the fianchetto. Quieter, positional play.
g3.right_feedback: O-O — castle. The Fianchetto KID is positional; expansion comes later.
g3.wrong_feedback: Against the Fianchetto KID (g3), O-O first is canonical. The fianchetto vs fianchetto setup is positional — you typically play c6 + Nbd7 + e5, slowly. Avoid premature e5 before castling.

when_ahead.plan: Convert the kingside attack — pawns roll forward.

when_equal.plan: Build the kingside attack patiently. Trade only if it helps the attack.
ideas: Reroute the knight to f4 or h5

when_behind.plan: Activate pieces. The dark bishop is your soul.

endgame_tips: The dark-square bishop is worth more than a passive rook.
King centralisation matters — use yours.
Passed pawns on the kingside can decide.

nimzo_indian_defense.name: Nimzo-Indian Defense
nimzo_indian_defense.summary: Black's most theoretically respected response to 1.d4. Pins the c3 knight with ...Bb4, giving up the bishop pair for damage to White's pawn structure (typically doubled c-pawns). One of the deepest, richest openings in chess — used by world champions for over a century.
golden_rules: Bb4 pinning the c3 knight is the defining move — accept that you'll trade the bishop for the knight.
Aim to compromise White's pawn structure (doubled c-pawns after Bxc3).
Your trumps: superior structure + flexibility. White's trumps: bishop pair + center.
Don't retreat the bishop without a reason — it serves its purpose on b4.

d4.right_feedback: Nf6 — flexible. Universal response to d4.

c4.name: Nimzo setup begins
c4.hint: Prepare Bb4 — the defining Nimzo move.
c4.right_feedback: e6 — prepares Bb4. Don't play g6 (that's the King's Indian).
c4.wrong_feedback: Against 2.c4, e6 prepares the Nimzo-Indian (3.Nc3 Bb4). g6 leads to the King's Indian (different opening, different plans). c5 invites the Benoni. e6 is the classical, theoretically-soundest response.

Nc3.name: Nimzo-Indian setup
Nc3.hint: Pin the knight to the king. This IS the Nimzo-Indian.
Nc3.right_feedback: Bb4 — pins the knight. White's c3 knight is now committed.
Nc3.wrong_feedback: After 3.Nc3, Bb4 is the defining Nimzo move — pins the knight, threatens to damage White's structure with Bxc3. Other moves (d5, Be7) lead to different openings (QGD-style positions). For the Nimzo, Bb4 is mandatory.

e3.name: Nimzo — Rubinstein Variation
e3.idea_opponent: White plays the calm Rubinstein — develops Nf3, Bd3, prepares O-O.
e3.right_feedback: O-O — castle. The Rubinstein is positional; both sides develop quietly.
e3.wrong_feedback: Against the Rubinstein (e3), O-O is the modern main line — castle first, decide later about Bxc3 or holding the pin. b6 (preparing Bb7) and c5 are also playable; O-O keeps maximum flexibility.

Qc2.name: Nimzo — Classical Variation
Qc2.idea_opponent: White plays Qc2 — protects c3 knight, avoids doubled pawns.
Qc2.right_feedback: O-O — develop calmly. The Classical Nimzo is rich; you'll play d5 or c5 later.
Qc2.wrong_feedback: Against the Classical Nimzo (Qc2), O-O is the modern main line. d5 (immediate central challenge) is also fine. The point of Qc2 was to avoid doubled c-pawns if Black plays Bxc3 — your bishop's value as a pin is reduced now, so castling first is sound.

a3.name: Nimzo — Sämisch Variation
a3.idea_opponent: White asks the bishop — accept doubled pawns or retreat?
a3.right_feedback: Bxc3+ — accept the trade, double White's c-pawns. This is the soul of the Nimzo.
a3.wrong_feedback: Against the Sämisch (a3), Bxc3+ is the Nimzo's principled move — give up the bishop, damage White's structure with doubled c-pawns. Retreating with Be7 wastes the entire opening idea (you'd be playing a worse QGD). Bxc3+ is the lesson the Nimzo teaches: structure over the bishop pair.

when_equal.plan: Exploit White's doubled c-pawns (or restricted bishops). Plan: d5 + c5 to open lines for your pieces, attack the weak pawns. Trade White's good bishop if possible.
ideas: Restrict White's light-square bishop with c4 (after b6 + Bb7).
Attack the doubled c-pawns with Na5 or Qa5.
Keep your knights — they're better than White's bishops in a closed structure.

when_ahead.plan: Open the position once you control the dark squares. Your superior structure wins endgames.
ideas: Trade queens if you have the structure advantage.

when_behind.plan: Close the position. The Nimzo's strength is solidity — if you're worse, dig in.

endgame_tips: Knight endings often favor Black after the Nimzo — your better structure compounds.
Bishop-vs-knight endings depend on pawn structure; closed positions favor the knight.

slav_defense.name: Slav Defense
slav_defense.summary: Support d5 with c6 instead of e6. Keeps the queen bishop free. Solid and respectable.
golden_rules: c6 holds d5 without locking in the bishop.
Develop the queen bishop OUTSIDE the pawn chain — to f5 or g4.
After dxc4, hold the pawn with b5 if you can.
Don't rush e6 — keep options open.

d4.right_feedback: d5 — meet White's pawn with your own.

c4.name: Queen's Gambit territory
c4.hint: Support d5 with the c-pawn instead of e6 (which would block your light-square bishop).
c4.right_feedback: c6 — the Slav. Keeps the light-square bishop's diagonal free.
c4.wrong_feedback: In the Slav Defense, c6 is the defining move — support d5 with the c-pawn so your light-square bishop can develop to f5 or g4 (unlike the QGD where e6 traps it). Playing e6 instead leads to the QGD, a completely different setup.

Nf3.name: Slav — Main
Nf3.idea_opponent: White develops, prepares to deal with the Slav structure.

Nc3.name: Slav — Main with Nc3
Nc3.hint: Take the pawn, plan to develop the light-square bishop to f5 next.
Nc3.right_feedback: dxc4 — accept the gambit. White will play a4 to stop ...b5, then you develop with Bf5.
Nc3.wrong_feedback: In the Slav Defense, dxc4 is the principled main line — the whole point of c6 was to enable this capture while keeping the light-square bishop free. After dxc4 a4 Bf5, your bishop is OUTSIDE the pawn chain — the Slav's biggest advantage over the QGD.

when_ahead.plan: Trade favourably. Solid pawn structure converts.

when_equal.plan: Develop calmly. Look for e5 or c5 breaks.

when_behind.plan: Stay solid. Slav is hard to crack.

endgame_tips: Solid pawns convert small advantages.
Bishop pair shines in open positions.
Centralise your king in the endgame.

english_opening.name: English Opening
english_opening.summary: Start with c4. Control d5 from a distance. Calm positional play, often with a fianchetto.
golden_rules: c4 controls d5 — no rush to push pawns in the centre.
Fianchetto the bishop to g2 — long diagonal at the queenside.
Develop knights to c3 and f3 before committing the centre.
Pawn breaks come later: e4, d4, or even b4.

c4.idea: Take queenside space, fight for d5 from the flank.
c4.hint: Develop the knight, fight for d5.

e5.name: English — Reversed Sicilian
e5.idea_opponent: Black plays in classical style — Sicilian Defense with colors reversed and a tempo more for you.

Nf6.name: English — Reversed Sicilian, main
Nf6.hint: Fianchetto the bishop — the English's signature move.
Nf6.right_feedback: g3 — prepares Bg2, the long-diagonal pressure that defines the English.
Nf6.wrong_feedback: In the English Opening, g3 is the signature move — the fianchetto puts your bishop on g2 where it pressures d5 and e4 along the long diagonal. Playing Nf3 first is OK but the fianchetto is what makes the English distinct from the Reti or other 1.Nf3 systems.

Nc6.name: English — Reversed Sicilian developed
Nc6.right_feedback: Bg2 — bishop on the long diagonal, eyes d5 and e4.

g6.name: English vs KID setup
g6.right_feedback: g3 — mirror the fianchetto. The English's symmetric setup is solid and flexible.

c5.name: Symmetrical English
c5.idea_opponent: Black mirrors — symmetrical, drawish but rich.
c5.right_feedback: Nc3 — develop. The Symmetrical English is positional; play patiently.

when_ahead.plan: Convert the queenside space advantage.

when_equal.plan: Manoeuvre patiently. Look for the right break.
ideas: d4 or e4 at the right moment

when_behind.plan: Stay flexible. The English is hard to attack.

endgame_tips: The fianchettoed bishop is your best endgame piece.
Knight outposts on d5 or e4 are killer.
Queenside majority converts to a passed pawn.

modern_defense.name: Modern Defense (Classical Setup)
modern_defense.summary: How to handle Black's Modern Defense (1...g6). Take the center with e4 + d4, develop Bc4 + Nf3 + O-O, push e5 to claim space, then ALWAYS support d4 with c3 — never Nbc3, which blocks the supporting pawn.
golden_rules: After d4 + e5, support the center with c3 — not Nbc3.
Nbc3 blocks the c-pawn permanently. The c-pawn needs c3 to support d4.
Develop Bc4 + Nf3 + O-O before pushing e5.
Black's Nc6 puts pressure on d4 — c3 is the structural answer.
After c3, plan Nbd2 + Bd3 / Bb3 + Re1 to complete development.

e4.right_feedback: Good — e4 grabs the center against the Modern.

g6.name: Modern Defense
g6.idea_opponent: Black fianchettos, will pressure your center from the flank.
g6.hint: Claim more space with the queen's pawn?
g6.right_feedback: Right — d4 gives you the big center.

Bg7.name: Fianchetto
Bg7.idea_opponent: Bishop aims at your d4-e5 chain.
Bg7.right_feedback: Bc4 — bishop on the long diagonal toward f7.

e6.name: Hybrid Setup with ...e6
e6.idea_opponent: Black solidifies the dark squares around the fianchetto.
e6.hint: Develop the knight, defend d4 indirectly.
e6.right_feedback: Nf3 — protects d4 from any future ...e5 / ...c5 break.

Nc6.name: Knight attacks d4
Nc6.idea_opponent: Black's knight presses on your d4 pawn.
Nc6.hint: Get the king safe before pushing forward.

Ne7.name: Knight reroute
Ne7.hint: Claim the e5 square — clamp the center.
Ne7.right_feedback: e5 — big center, Black's knight on e7 is now passive.

a6.name: Queenside prep
a6.idea_opponent: Black prepares ...b5 to harass your Bc4.
a6.hint: In the Modern Defense, Black's knight on c6 attacks your d4. How do you defend d4 without blocking your own pawn?
a6.right_feedback: In the Modern Defense, c3 supports your d4 pawn — keeps the big center solid. Your b1-knight can come to d2 next.
a6.wrong_feedback: In the Modern Defense, the idea is: c3 (the pawn) supports your d4 + e5 center. Nc3 blocks the c-pawn for good — now d4 has no pawn behind it. Black plays ...d6 then ...dxe5 and your big center falls apart.

when_equal.plan: After c3 + Nbd2, expand with Bd3 (or Bb3) + Re1 + h3 + a4 — patient development.
ideas: Trade Black's fianchetto bishop if you can win a tempo doing it.
Watch for Black's ...d6 / ...d5 break — meet ...d5 with exd6 e.p. when available.

when_ahead.plan: Open the center decisively with d5 or e6. Black's king is still in the centre.
ideas: Trade queens only if the resulting endgame is winning.
Push the kingside pawns to open lines toward the black king.

when_behind.plan: Keep the position closed. Black's fianchetto is the strong piece — neutralize it.
ideas: Avoid pawn breaks until you've consolidated.

endgame_tips: Your d4-e5 chain becomes a queenside majority in pawn endings — push the queenside.
Black's dark-square bishop is the key piece; trade it for any meaningful concession.

philidor_defense.name: Philidor Defense
philidor_defense.summary: How to handle Black's Philidor Defense (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6). Black plays passively, supporting e5 with the d-pawn. Punish this by opening the center immediately with 3.d4 — your space advantage often persists into the middlegame and endgame.
golden_rules: Open the center with 3.d4 — Black's setup is passive, exploit the space.
After 3...exd4, recapture with the knight (4.Nxd4), keeping pieces active.
Bc4 aims at f7 — even more effective here since Black's king has less support.
Don't trade pieces — Black wants simplification, you want activity.

d6.name: Philidor Defense
d6.idea_opponent: Black defends e5 passively — cramped but solid.
d6.hint: Black's setup is passive. How do you punish it?
d6.right_feedback: d4 — opens the center against Black's cramped position.
d6.wrong_feedback: In the Philidor Defense, the idea is: open the center with d4 — Black has chosen a passive setup, exploit the space they gave up. Bc4 or Nc3 first let Black consolidate; d4 immediately is the punishment.

exd4.name: Philidor — Main Line
exd4.right_feedback: Nxd4 — strong central knight, more space than Black.
exd4.wrong_feedback: In the Philidor, Nxd4 is right. Qxd4 lets Black gain a tempo with Nc6 hitting your queen.

Nf6.name: Philidor — Hanham
Nf6.idea_opponent: Black holds the center, planning Nbd7 + Be7.
Nf6.right_feedback: Nc3 — develops, supports e4. Plan Bc4 + O-O next.
Nf6.wrong_feedback: In the Philidor Hanham, Nc3 is natural development. Don't push d5 yet — closing the center helps Black who has less space. Develop first.

when_equal.plan: Develop calmly with Bc4 + Nc3 + O-O + h3. Black has less space — patient play wins.
ideas: Don't trade pieces — Black wants simplification.
Black's Be7 / Bd6 bishop is passive; trade your worst piece for it if convenient.

when_ahead.plan: Open lines on the kingside — Black's king is the weakest spot in their cramped position.
ideas: Pawn storm on the kingside if Black castled there.
Trade queens only when the endgame is clearly winning.

when_behind.plan: Simplify and aim for a draw — Black's positional advantages are usually minimal.
ideas: Avoid weak squares around the king.

endgame_tips: Your space advantage often persists — keep pieces active.
Black's bishops often end up on bad squares (e7, d7) — exploit this in piece endings.

bishops_opening.name: Bishop's Opening
bishops_opening.summary: 1.e4 e5 2.Bc4. Italian-family opening — aim the bishop at f7 immediately. Often transposes to the Italian Game after 3.Nf3. Modern lines also include the Vienna-Anti-Petroff with 2...Nf6 3.d3 or 3.d4.
golden_rules: Bc4 first, then choose: Nf3 (transposes to Italian) or d3 (Modern Bishop's Opening, slow positional).
Against ...Nf6, d3 (Modern) is solid; 2.Nf3 first transposes to standard Italian Two Knights.
Castle kingside, develop knights to f3 and d2 (or c3) — quiet positional play.
Don't push d4 too early without c3 support.

e5.name: Open Game
e5.hint: Aim the bishop at f7 right away.
e5.right_feedback: Bc4 — Bishop's Opening. Eyes f7 immediately, before developing the knight.
e5.wrong_feedback: In the Bishop's Opening, Bc4 is the defining move — bishop aims at f7 before knights come out. Nf3 first leads to standard Italian (also fine, just different order). Bc4 first leaves you the flexibility of d3 (Modern Bishop's) or Nc3 (Vienna-style).

Nf6.name: Bishop's Opening — Berlin / Modern
Nf6.hint: Defend e4 with a pawn — Modern Bishop's Opening setup.
Nf6.right_feedback: d3 — Modern Bishop's Opening. Solid positional play; Nf3 + O-O + Nbd2 next.
Nf6.wrong_feedback: Against 2...Nf6 in the Bishop's Opening, d3 is the modern positional choice — defends e4 and prepares slow development. Nf3 transposes to the Two Knights Defense (Fried Liver territory, sharper). Both sound; d3 if you prefer quiet positional games.

Bc5.name: Bishop's Opening → Italian transposition
Bc5.idea_opponent: Black mirrors with Bc5 — typically transposes to Italian.
Bc5.right_feedback: Nf3 — develops, transposes to Italian Giuoco Piano.

when_equal.plan: Slow positional play. Bc4 + d3 + Nf3 + O-O + Nbd2 + Re1. Eventually push c3 + d4 if Black allows.
ideas: Don't push d4 without c3 support.
Keep the bishop on c4 (or b3 if attacked by ...Na5).
Plan f4 or g4 expansion if Black castles short.

when_ahead.plan: Open the center with d4 once supported. Trade pieces if your structure is better.
ideas: Push d4 + e5 with c3 support.
Trade queens if endgame favors you.

when_behind.plan: Keep the position closed. The Bishop's Opening is rarely won by Black quickly.
ideas: Don't trade the bishop on c4 for the knight.

endgame_tips: The bishop pair (if you keep both) gives an endgame edge — preserve them.
Pawn structures from Bishop's Opening transpositions usually resemble Italian endgames.

vienna_game.name: Vienna Game
vienna_game.summary: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3. Develop the queen's knight first, then choose: Vienna Gambit (3.f4) for sharp attacking play, Bc4 (Italian-style) for solid positional play, or g3 (fianchetto) for hypermodern setups. Often transposes to Italian or King's Gambit territory.
golden_rules: Nc3 first, then commit: f4 (Vienna Gambit, sharp) or Bc4 (Italian-style, quiet).
The Vienna Gambit (3.f4) is sharp — only play it if you've studied the lines.
Bc4 + d3 + Nf3 + O-O is the calm path, transposes to Italian.
Don't play Bg5 too early — Black can chase the bishop with h6.

e5.name: Open Game
e5.hint: Develop the queen's knight first — the Vienna Game.
e5.right_feedback: Nc3 — Vienna Game. Develops the queen's knight before the king's knight.
e5.wrong_feedback: In the Vienna Game, Nc3 is the defining move — queen's knight first. Nf3 transposes to Italian/Ruy/Scotch (all fine, just different openings). Bc4 leads to Bishop's Opening. For the Vienna, Nc3 first.

Nf6.name: Vienna — Main
Nf6.hint: Italian-style: aim the bishop at f7. Or play f4 (Vienna Gambit) for sharp attack.
Nf6.right_feedback: Bc4 — quiet Vienna. Now plan d3 + Nf3 + O-O. (f4 is the Vienna Gambit — sharper alternative.)
Nf6.wrong_feedback: Against 2...Nf6, you have a real choice: Bc4 (quiet, Italian-style) or f4 (Vienna Gambit — sharp, theoretically OK but requires study). g3 (Fianchetto) is also valid. Pick based on style. For 1200-1500 players, Bc4 is the safer choice.

when_equal.plan: Develop calmly: d3 + Nf3 + O-O + Nbd2 + Re1. Vienna positions are slow positional games unless you commit to the Gambit.
ideas: Don't push f4 unless you have a clear attacking plan.
Trade the bishop on c4 for Black's knight only if you get something concrete.
Build up slowly with f3 + g3 + h3 + Kg2 as the king cluster.

when_ahead.plan: Push f4-f5 to expand on the kingside. Vienna structures naturally lead to kingside attacks.
ideas: Push f4 then f5 to open lines.
Sacrifice pieces for the king attack if calculation works.

when_behind.plan: Trade pieces, simplify. The Vienna is rarely lost from solid positions.

endgame_tips: Vienna endings often resemble Italian — same pawn structures, same plans.
Bishop pair is the key asset if you keep both.

englund_gambit_response.name: Englund Gambit Response
englund_gambit_response.summary: After 1.d4 e5 (Englund Gambit by Black), the principled response is 2.dxe5 — accept the pawn. Black has dubious compensation; if they try the Englund Gambit Mate Trap (2...Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7 4.Bf4?? Qb4+ winning the b2 pawn or worse), white must NOT play 4.Bf4. Develop normally with 3.Nf3 and 4.Nc3 or 4.Bf4-with-care.
golden_rules: Accept the gambit: 2.dxe5 — take the pawn.
Watch for the Englund Mate Trap: after 2...Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7, do NOT play 4.Bf4 (loses to Qb4+).
Develop calmly with Nf3 + Nc3 + e3 — don't try to keep all the extra material.
Black usually has minimal compensation for the pawn — convert the endgame patiently.

e5.name: Englund Gambit
e5.idea_opponent: Black sacrifices the e-pawn for dubious initiative.
e5.hint: Take the pawn. Black's gambit is theoretically losing.
e5.right_feedback: dxe5 — accept the gambit. Black has minimal compensation.
e5.wrong_feedback: Against the Englund Gambit (1...e5), dxe5 is the principled response — take the pawn. The Englund is theoretically unsound; you should win a pawn cleanly. Refusing with c4 or Nf3 is OK but accepting is sharper.

Qe7.name: Englund — Mate Trap attempt
Qe7.idea_opponent: Black sets up the Englund Mate Trap (Qb4+ next).
Qe7.hint: Develop the queen's knight — and AVOID Bf4 which loses to Qb4+.
Qe7.right_feedback: Nc3 — develop safely. NOT Bf4 (which would lose to Qb4+ winning b2 pawn or queen).
Qe7.wrong_feedback: In the Englund Mate Trap, Nc3 is correct. Bf4?? is the famous trap — Black plays Qb4+ and you lose the b2 pawn (or worse, the queen if you block with Qd2 Qxb2 winning). Nc3 develops safely AND defends b4 indirectly.

when_equal.plan: Convert the extra pawn. Trade pieces, simplify, win the endgame.

when_ahead.plan: You're up a pawn from the start. Push the queenside majority in the endgame.
ideas: Push a4-a5 or b4 to create a passed pawn.
Trade pieces to reach a winning endgame.

when_behind.plan: Shouldn't happen if you avoided the Englund Mate Trap. If it does, defend solidly.

endgame_tips: Up-a-pawn endings: trade pieces, push passed pawns.
The Englund Gambit's pawn advantage typically persists into the endgame.
